scenes.text: A photo taken on a dark December night. Can a map built on an overcast day say where the camera stood?
scenes.say: A photo, taken on a dark December night in Oxford. Can a map built on an overcast day say exactly where the camera stood?

scenes.headline: How visual positioning turns one photo into a pose
scenes.sub: MultiSet on RobotCar Seasons, and what its video can and cannot show
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Halvard! Today: how a visual positioning system finds a camera from a single picture, and how to read a demo of one.

scenes.title: A map that remembers
scenes.say: Chapter one. A map that remembers.

steps.term: Descriptor: a vector that summarises a patch
steps.say: Start with one overcast November drive. In every image, find key points, and describe the patch around each as a vector.
Match those features between overlapping images, then triangulate each match into a point in space. Bundle adjustment refines every camera and every point together.
Out comes a cloud of 3D points, each keeping the descriptors it was seen with. That memory lets a new photo find it again.
This is the benchmark's map of an Oxford square, built from the reference drive.
And these are query photos of the same building: sun, night, snow, and low sun that washes everything out.

scenes.title: One photo, one pose
scenes.say: Chapter two. One photo, one pose.

steps.term: Retrieval: find map images that look alike
steps.say: First, retrieval. One vector for the whole photo, compared with every map image, returns the few most alike. A city shrinks to a street.
Then local matching. Each query feature that matches a feature of a mapped point becomes a correspondence: this pixel shows that point.

steps.term: PnP: pose from points and their pixels
steps.say: Finally, Perspective-n-Point solves for the rotation and position that project those points onto their pixels. Three good correspondences are enough.

params.map: the map, from the overcast drive
labels: A query: each match is a ray
Three rays, one pose, count who agrees
Night: few good rays, a wrong pose
Learned features: enough good rays again

steps.say: Seen from above, the map is two rows of facade points along the street.
A query photo's matches are rays from the camera. Most end on the point they claim. Some are wrong, and point at nothing.
RANSAC draws three rays at random, solves a pose, and counts how many other rays that pose explains. The pose with the most support wins.
At night most rays are wrong. A triple with a bad ray can win the vote, and the pose lands somewhere else entirely.
Learned features bring enough good rays back. The vote finds the true pose again, and the inliers light up.

scenes.title: How many draws RANSAC needs

parts.note: chance a random triple is all good
parts.say: If a share w of the matches is right, a random triple is clean with probability w cubed.
N is how many triples you must draw to see one clean triple. At seventy percent good, about eleven. At ten percent, over four thousand.

scenes.say: This is why conditions matter: they set the share of good matches.

scenes.title: What night does
scenes.say: Chapter three. What night does to a feature.

scenes.title: Active Search in 2018, within 0.25 m and 2°
scenes.say: In the benchmark paper, a standard hand-crafted method placed about half of rain queries within twenty-five centimetres. At night, half a percent.

steps.say: With learned features, night queries can succeed. Here, a dark query and its daytime map image share many consistent matches.

steps.term: Failure one: retrieval picks the wrong place
steps.say: But there are two ways to fail. Retrieval can return the wrong place,

steps.term: Failure two: too few good matches
steps.say: or the right place can yield too few good matches for the vote.

scenes.title: Night queries within 0.25 m and 2°, v2 board
scenes.say: Today the public board's night column runs from about forty percent for the standard single-camera pipeline to sixty-six for the best row.

scenes.title: What the video shows
scenes.say: Chapter four. What MultiSet's video shows.

steps.say: MultiSet built its map from the overcast day, then localised photos from nine other drives across a year. Here is the dry night drive of December the tenth.
Each card prints the error from the reference pose. These three night queries land eighteen to twenty-four centimetres off.

scenes.label: Showcased queries inside 0.25 m and 2°
scenes.say: All twenty-seven showcased queries fall inside the finest threshold. Those are good results for those photos.

scenes.label: odds that 27 random queries all pass, at the top row's rates
scenes.say: But they were chosen for a video. At the best row's rates, twenty-seven random queries would all pass about once in twenty-seven thousand tries.

scenes.title: What the video does not say
scenes.say: So here is what is missing.

items.say: There is no recall, the share of all queries that pass.
No row on the public board connects to MultiSet.
The cards need reference poses, so these are probably from the half whose poses are public.
And the reference poses carry their own error, about the size of the numbers on the cards.

scenes.title: Photos on a site
scenes.sub: The job site people asked for
scenes.say: Chapter five. Photos that land where they were taken.

steps.say: At a trade show, plant and site people asked for two jobs: photos that land where they were taken, and finding the equipment they were sent to fix.
On a site, the hard cases are repeated floors and a scene that changes every week. RobotCar tests neither, so measure on your own held-out photos.

scenes.text: A VPS is retrieval, matching and a RANSAC vote. A benchmark's value is its denominator; the video left it out.

recap: The map: 3D points that keep descriptors
The pose: matches, then a RANSAC vote
The demo: successes, not a recall
scenes.say: The map remembers, RANSAC votes, and a demo shows successes, not a rate. Thanks for watching!
